contentBlocks.text: Yesterday you found pushes and pulls all around you. But what happens when two forces act on the same object at the same time? Sometimes nothing moves at all — and sometimes something moves fast. Let's find out why.

When forces on an object are balanced (equal in strength, opposite in direction), the object doesn't change its motion — like two evenly matched teams in tug-of-war, the rope stays still. When forces are unbalanced (one side is stronger), the object moves in the direction of the stronger force — the rope slides toward the stronger team. Try this: hold a book flat on your open hand. Gravity pulls it down; your hand pushes it up. Since the book stays still, are those forces balanced or unbalanced? Now tilt your hand — the book slides off. What changed?
Balanced forces keep things steady. Unbalanced forces cause a change in motion. Tomorrow we'll use this idea to predict how objects will move.

objectives: Distinguish balanced forces (no change in motion) from unbalanced forces (motion changes)
Explain a real, hands-on example of each using gravity and a supporting force
materialsNeeded: A book or other flat object
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review push/pull from yesterday.
2. Introduce the tug-of-war analogy for balanced vs. unbalanced forces.
3. Do the book-on-hand demonstration: flat hand (balanced), then tilt (unbalanced) — narrate what's happening to the forces each time.
4. Try 2-3 more examples together: a parked car (balanced — brakes push back against gravity/friction), a rolling ball slowing down (unbalanced — friction is stronger than the push that started it).
5. Complete the worksheet, sorting scenarios as balanced or unbalanced.
6. Close by asking the child to invent their own balanced-force example.
differentiationTips: Struggling: stick to the single book-on-hand example repeated with variations before introducing new scenarios
Ready for more: introduce the term 'net force' informally — the 'leftover' force after balanced ones cancel out
Hands-on learners benefit most from physically doing the tilt demonstration multiple times, narrating aloud each time
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. Book resting flat on a table = balanced. 2. Tilted book sliding off = unbalanced. 3. A parked car with the brake on = balanced. 4. A rolling ball slowing to a stop = unbalanced (friction).
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses NGSS 3-PS2-1: planning and reasoning about the effects of balanced and unbalanced forces on an object's motion, the core Grade 3 forces standard.

generationData.instructions: For each scenario, write BALANCED (motion stays the same) or UNBALANCED (motion changes).

A tilted book sliding off a table
A parked car with the brake on
